title: Sensitivity Analyses
text:
Two pre-specified sensitivity analyses were conducted for CMV to address era effects and donor-type heterogeneity.


Show code
sens_list <- list(
  or_summary(post_m1, "b_ptcy_binary", "Full corpus", model = "Primary")
)
if (!is.null(post_m1_post2020)) {
  sens_list[[length(sens_list)+1]] <- or_summary(post_m1_post2020, "b_ptcy_binary", "Post-2020", model = "Post-2020")
}
if (!is.null(post_m1_haplo)) {
  sens_list[[length(sens_list)+1]] <- or_summary(post_m1_haplo, "b_ptcy_binary", "Haplo-only", model = "Haplo \u226550%")
}
sens_cmv <- do.call(rbind, sens_list) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(
    model = factor(model, levels = rev(c("Primary (k=22)", "Post-2020 (k=17)", "Haplo \u226550% (k=12)"))),
    label = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", or, lo, hi)
  )

ggplot(sens_cmv, aes(x = or, y = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = jama_grey) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), colour = jama_navy, fill = jama_navy,
                  shape = 16, size = 0.6, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(x = hi, label = label), hjust = -0.1, size = 3.2, colour = jama_black) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.8, 3)) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 1.5, 2, 2.5)) +
  labs(x = "Odds Ratio (log scale)", y = NULL,
       title = "CMV Sensitivity — Comparison 1",
       subtitle = "Restricting to post-2020 or haplo-dominant studies strengthens the signal") +
  theme_jama()








Figure 1: CMV sensitivity analyses (C1). All three estimates use post-Block-9 data. Both subgroup restrictions strengthen the signal, consistent with (a) letermovir-era studies widening the gap and (b) haploidentical settings amplifying the T-cell depletion effect.

Comparison 2: Expanded Arm Inclusion
The primary C2 analysis excluded 12 arms (PTCy+ATG combo, mixed, neither). The sensitivity reclassifies PTCy+ATG as PTCy-side and mixed-ATG arms by PTCy co-administration status, adding 6 previously unpaired studies.

title: Sensitivity Analyses
section: Comparison 2: Haplo Proportion as Effect Modifier
text:
Comparison 2: Haplo Proportion as Effect Modifier
The proportion of haploidentical donors in the PTCy arm varies substantially across C2 studies (0–100%). We tested whether this modifies the PTCy-vs-ATG treatment effect via frequentist meta-regression with haplo_pct as a continuous moderator.


Show code
plot_metareg <- function(es_df, fit, outcome_label) {
  df <- data.frame(
    haplo_pct = es_df$haplo_pct,
    or = exp(es_df$yi),
    wi = 1 / es_df$vi
  )

  newdat <- data.frame(haplo_pct = seq(0, 100, 1))
  pred <- predict(fit, newmods = newdat$haplo_pct)
  pred_df <- data.frame(haplo_pct = newdat$haplo_pct,
                         or = exp(pred$pred),
                         lo = exp(pred$ci.lb),
                         hi = exp(pred$ci.ub))

  ggplot(df, aes(x = haplo_pct, y = or)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = jama_grey) +
    geom_ribbon(data = pred_df, aes(y = or, ymin = lo, ymax = hi),
                alpha = 0.15, fill = jama_navy) +
    geom_line(data = pred_df, aes(y = or), colour = jama_navy, linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_point(aes(size = wi), colour = jama_navy, alpha = 0.7) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    scale_size_continuous(range = c(1.5, 6), guide = "none") +
    labs(x = "Haplo donor %", y = "Odds Ratio",
         title = outcome_label,
         subtitle = sprintf("p = %.3f, R\u00B2 = %.0f%%", fit$QMp, fit$R2)) +
    theme_jama(base_size = 10)
}

library(patchwork)
plot_metareg(mr_es_os, fit_mr_os, "OS") +
  plot_metareg(mr_es_cmv, fit_mr_cmv, "CMV") +
  plot_metareg(mr_es_agvhd, fit_mr_agvhd, "aGVHD") +
  plot_annotation(title = "Meta-Regression: Haplo Proportion as Moderator (C2, Primary Dataset)")








Figure 4: Meta-regression of PTCy-vs-ATG treatment effect on haplo donor proportion. Each bubble is a study (size ∝ precision). The blue line and shaded band show the REML-estimated slope and 95% CI. aGVHD shows a significant positive slope (p = 0.035, R² = 47%): the PTCy advantage over ATG attenuates as haplo proportion increases.

NoteInterpretation



When PTCy is used with matched donors (0% haplo), the aGVHD advantage over ATG is large (predicted OR 0.34 [0.17–0.68]). At 100% haplo, this advantage is fully attenuated (OR 1.22 [0.52–2.91]). This is mechanistically coherent: HLA mismatch–driven alloreactivity in haplo transplants partially overwhelms the differential GVHD-suppressive benefit of PTCy relative to ATG. OS shows a suggestive but non-significant trend in the same direction (p = 0.13). CMV is unmoderated by donor type.
This finding was confirmed on both the primary C2 dataset (shown here, k = 8) and the sensitivity dataset including PTCy+ATG combo arms (k = 14, p = 0.039, R² = 31%).
Conditioning intensity. An additive model including both haplo proportion and MAC-predominant conditioning (k = 8, 1 study dropped for missing data) increased R² to 73%. The haplo coefficient strengthened (β = 0.015, p = 0.005) while the MAC term was suggestive but non-significant (β = −0.68, p = 0.14), pointing toward a possible independent MAC-associated enhancement of PTCy’s relative GVHD advantage. Importantly, haplo and MAC are not confounded — they pull in opposite directions — and the haplo moderator is robust to conditioning adjustment. A formal interaction term was not estimable at this sample size.

text:
Publication Bias: RoBMA
Robust Bayesian model-averaging (RoBMA) jointly tests for the presence of an effect, heterogeneity, and publication bias by averaging across models with and without each component. P(effect) is the posterior probability that the true effect is non-zero; P(pub bias) is the posterior probability that selection models improve fit; BF(bias) is the corresponding inclusion Bayes factor.


Show code

  robma_tbl |>
    kable(row.names = FALSE,

          align = c("l","c","c","c","c","c","c")) |>
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = TRUE)
} else {

WarningPublication Bias Assessment



RoBMA identifies strong evidence of publication bias for C1 OS (BF = 10.9) and C1 aGVHD (BF = 14.1), and moderate evidence for C2 OS (BF = 5.2) and C2 aGVHD (BF = 4.1). After bias adjustment, model-averaged posterior probabilities of a non-null effect are below 50% for all outcomes.
This does not mean the effects are definitively absent — it means the current evidence base cannot reliably distinguish true effects from publication-bias artifacts under RoBMA’s default skeptical priors (Normal(0, 1) on log-OR, 50% prior mass on the null). The bias evidence is strongest for the two outcomes with the largest apparent effects (C1 OS, C1 aGVHD), consistent with selective reporting amplifying favourable results in non-randomised comparisons. C1 CMV and C1 NRM show no meaningful evidence of bias (BF < 1).

title: Comparison 3: Within-PTCy Regimen Variants
text: Comparison 3 evaluates within-PTCy regimen variants — comparing different PTCy-based platforms (e.g., PTCy + tacrolimus/MMF vs PTCy + sirolimus, or PTCy alone vs PTCy + CNI). Unlike C1 and C2, this comparison tests whether the choice of backbone immunosuppression alongside PTCy matters, rather than whether PTCy itself is beneficial.

M1 (Direct effect): OR 0.79 (95% CrI 0.73–0.85), P(OR < 1) = 100%, τ = 0.61. The posterior is entirely below the null, indicating a consistent mortality reduction with PTCy.
M2 (Steroid-adjusted): Adjusting for arm-level systemic steroid exposure attenuated the OR from 0.79 to 0.86 (95% CrI 0.77–0.96), a 36% reduction in the log-OR. The residual benefit after adjustment indicates GVHD mediation does not fully explain the OS advantage.

Figure 2: Posterior density for the PTCy log-OR on non-relapse mortality. M2 adjustment abolishes the M1 benefit entirely — the hallmark of complete steroid mediation.





M1: OR 0.88 (95% CrI 0.66–1.18), P(OR < 1) = 83%, τ = 0.72. Directionally favourable but CrI crosses null; k decreased from 15 (pre-Block-9) to 12 after arm reclassification.
M2: OR 0.90 (95% CrI 0.59–1.36), P(OR < 1) = 60%. The M1→M2 shift is modest (0.88 → 0.90), with wide CrIs overlapping substantially. Unlike the pre-Block-9 analysis (where M2 crossed null at 1.02, suggesting complete mediation), the current data are inconclusive regarding steroid mediation of NRM — the point estimates barely differ, and the wide intervals accommodate both full mediation and no mediation.






NoteNRM Mediation — Revised



The pre-Block-9 M1→M2 shift (OR 0.86 → 1.02) was the strongest mediation finding. After arm reclassification and expanded data, the shift is now minimal (0.88 → 0.90) with wide CrIs. The steroid mediation hypothesis for NRM remains plausible but is no longer clearly supported by the Bayesian models alone.

Figure 5: Posterior densities for the PTCy effect on chronic GVHD. Moderate-severe NIH cGVHD (navy) is the primary grading; any-NIH cGVHD (grey) is shown for completeness.





Moderate-severe NIH cGVHD (k = 21): OR 0.33 (95% CrI 0.29–0.36), P(OR < 1) = 100%, τ = 0.71. The largest treatment effect in the entire analysis — PTCy reduces moderate-severe chronic GVHD by approximately two-thirds compared to CNI+MTX/MMF. The CrI is narrow and entirely below null, reflecting the large k and consistent direction across studies.
Any-NIH cGVHD (k = 8): OR 0.23 (95% CrI 0.18–0.30), P(OR < 1) = 100%, τ = 0.52. An even larger effect when including all grades, though k is smaller. The lower OR likely reflects the inclusion of mild cGVHD, which PTCy prevents almost completely.






NotecGVHD: The Strongest PTCy Effect



Chronic GVHD is the most profoundly affected outcome in the entire analysis. The moderate-severe cGVHD OR of 0.33 is substantially larger than the aGVHD effect (OR 0.67), consistent with PTCy’s mechanism: alloreactive T-cell depletion during the early post-transplant window has an outsized impact on the chronic alloimmune processes that drive cGVHD. This has direct implications for long-term quality of life, immunosuppression duration, and late NRM.

Figure 8: Posterior density for the PTCy effect on relapse-related mortality (C1). M1 and M2 (steroid-adjusted) are near-identical, indicating no steroid mediation — consistent with a direct graft-versus-leukaemia mechanism.





M1: OR 0.84 (95% CrI 0.76–0.93), P(OR < 1) > 99%, k = 38. PTCy is associated with reduced relapse-related mortality, consistent with preserved graft-versus-leukaemia (GVL) activity. This is the first meta-analytic estimate of this outcome.
M2 (steroid-adjusted): OR 0.83 (95% CrI 0.73–0.93). No attenuation after steroid adjustment — confirming that the RRM benefit operates through a GVHD-independent pathway, most plausibly GVL preservation. This contrasts with OS (partially mediated) and NRM (uncertain mediation), and helps decompose the residual OS benefit that survives steroid adjustment.






NoteRRM Completes the Causal Picture



The RRM finding resolves the question of what drives the residual OS benefit after steroid adjustment. OS M2 retains ~64% of the M1 log-OR; RRM retains ~100%. The portion of the OS advantage not explained by GVHD/steroid reduction is likely attributable to preserved anti-leukaemia immunity.

ImportantBK Virus: Dual Mechanism



Unlike CMV and BSI (which operate through T-cell lymphodepletion alone), BK virus reactivation has a dual mechanism: (1) direct urothelial toxicity from cyclophosphamide metabolites (acrolein), and (2) impaired BK-specific immune reconstitution. This explains why the BK effect (OR 2.48) is larger than CMV (OR 1.26) and BSI (OR 1.87).

Figure 10: Posterior density for the PTCy effect on infection-related mortality (C1). The distribution is centred above OR = 1, indicating higher IRM with PTCy — but this conflicts with the frequentist null (see text).





Bayesian M1: OR 1.35 (95% CrI 1.16–1.57), P(OR > 1) = 100%, k = 16, τ = 0.84. The Bayesian binomial model finds elevated infection-related mortality with PTCy.
Frequentist RE: OR 1.01 (95% CI 0.70–1.45), I² = 70%. The frequentist random-effects model finds a null effect.






WarningBayesian–Frequentist Divergence



The Bayesian and frequentist models disagree on C1 IRM. The divergence is driven by two large CIBMTR registry studies (Battipaglia 2019: IRM 41% vs 25%; Mulroney 2021: IRM 35% vs 26%) that together contribute >2,400 patients. The Bayesian binomial model weights these heavily (they carry the most binomial information); the frequentist RE model equalizes study contributions through the random-effects structure, and smaller studies showing protective effects (Baron 2024, Montoro 2021, Tischer 2015) partially offset the CIBMTR signal.
Interpretation: The truth likely lies between these estimates. PTCy may modestly increase infection-related mortality (consistent with the Bayesian estimate), but the effect is uncertain and substantially smaller than the infection rate increases (CMV +26%, BSI +87%, BK +148%). The key message remains that the infection rate excess translates to a much smaller — and possibly null — mortality excess.

title: Post-Transplant Cyclophosphamide Meta-Analysis
text:
Background. Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) has become widely adopted for GVHD prophylaxis in allogeneic haematopoietic cell transplantation, yet comprehensive quantitative evidence synthesis across survival, GVHD, and infection outcomes — and across comparator regimens — has been lacking.
Methods. We conducted a Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of 251 studies (14 RCTs) comparing PTCy to (1) CNI+MTX/MMF-based regimens (Comparison 1), (2) ATG-based regimens (Comparison 2), and (3) within-PTCy regimen variants (Comparison 3). The dashed vertical line marks OR = 1 (no effect). OR < 1 favours PTCy for mortality, GVHD, and IFI outcomes.






Key Findings

1. Chronic GVHD — the largest treatment effect. PTCy reduced moderate-severe chronic GVHD by two-thirds vs CNI+MTX (C1 OR 0.33 [95% CrI 0.29–0.36], k = 21). This is the largest treatment effect in the analysis — substantially exceeding acute GVHD (OR 0.67) — with direct implications for long-term quality of life and immunosuppression duration. The effect attenuates vs ATG (C2 OR 0.79), consistent with ATG also providing cGVHD prophylaxis.


2. Survival and acute GVHD benefit. PTCy was associated with reduced overall mortality (C1 OR 0.79; C2 OR 0.82) and acute GVHD grade II–IV (C1 OR 0.67; C2 OR 0.58) in both comparisons. Effects were consistent across comparators.


3. Anti-relapse benefit preserved. RRM was reduced in both comparisons (C1 OR 0.83; C2 OR 0.79) with no steroid mediation, supporting preserved graft-versus-leukaemia activity.


4. Infections increased but infection-related mortality not clearly elevated. CMV, BSI, and BK virus rates were elevated vs CNI+MTX. However, infection-related mortality was not clearly increased (C1 Bayesian OR 1.35 [Bayesian–frequentist discordant]; C2 OR 0.9). The infectious morbidity appears manageable and does not translate proportionally into death.


5. CMV depletion gradient. PTCy increased CMV vs CNI+MTX (OR 1.26) but was near-null vs ATG (OR 0.98), supporting a T-cell depletion depth gradient (CNI < PTCy ≈ ATG) rather than a PTCy-specific effect.


6. Within-PTCy variants equivalent. C3 found no significant differences across PTCy regimen variants for any outcome, suggesting the PTCy component dominates the regimen effect.

Mechanistic Framework
The findings resolve into a framework built on three separable consequences of PTCy:

GVHD suppression pathway (intended): PTCy eliminates alloreactive T cells → reduced aGVHD (OR 0.67) and profoundly reduced cGVHD (OR 0.33) → less steroid exposure → lower NRM → improved OS. Chronic GVHD is the most affected outcome, consistent with PTCy’s early alloreactive depletion having an outsized impact on chronic alloimmune processes.
GVL preservation pathway (intended): PTCy → reduced relapse-related mortality (C1 OR 0.84; C2 OR 0.79), steroid-independent. This explains the residual OS advantage after GVHD/steroid adjustment.
T-cell lymphodepletion pathway (unintended): PTCy depletes pathogen-specific T cells during engraftment → elevated CMV, BSI, and BK virus. The CMV depletion gradient (CNI < PTCy ≈ ATG) confirms this is a relative depth-of-depletion effect. BK virus has an additional urothelial toxicity component. Critically, the elevated infection rates do not translate clearly into elevated infection-related mortality, suggesting the infectious cost is clinically manageable.

title: Model Diagnostics
text:
Prior Sensitivity
The half-normal(0, 0.50) prior on τ was chosen based on plausible heterogeneity in transplant outcomes. The prior places 95% of its mass below τ = 0.98, which corresponds to a range of study-level ORs spanning roughly 0.14 to 7.1 around the pooled estimate — generous for transplant outcomes.
For the PTCy coefficient, the Normal(0, 0.82) prior corresponds to 95% prior mass between OR 0.20 and 5.0, ensuring the prior does not materially constrain the posterior in any outcome.






TipAssessing Prior Influence



The Bayesian τ estimates are most informative for outcomes with k ≥ 15 (OS, RRM, aGVHD in C1). For sparse outcomes (BSI k=6, NRM C2 k=2), the prior provides meaningful regularisation — this is a feature, not a bug, as it prevents extreme heterogeneity estimates that would arise from fitting random-effects models to very small corpora.

title: Discussion
text:
The totality of findings across six pre-specified outcomes and two independent comparisons informs a mechanistic framework built on the distinction between two immunological consequences of PTCy.


PTCy eliminates alloreactive T cells during the critical window of allorecognition, reducing acute GVHD grade II–IV across both comparisons. This propagates downstream:

NRM benefit shows steroid mediation in both comparisons
OS benefit is only partially mediated, suggesting an additional direct contribution — most plausibly graft-versus-leukaemia preservation




The same cyclophosphamide pulse depletes the nascent CMV- and bacterial-specific T-cell repertoire. This manifests as elevated infection risk — but the magnitude and direction depend on the comparator’s own depletion depth.

section: CMV: Evidence for the Depletion Hierarchy
text:
CMV: Evidence for the Depletion Hierarchy

Primary analysis
C1 CMV remains consistently harmful: PTCy increases CMV reactivation vs CNI+MTX/MMF (OR 1.26 [1.07–1.47]). In C2, the point estimate is directionally protective (OR 0.98 [0.78–1.24]), but the CrI crosses null. The qualitative direction reversal reported in the pre-Block-9 analysis (C2 OR 0.77 [0.60–0.99]) is attenuated.


Show code
tibble(
  `C1: vs CNI+MTX` = post_m1$b_ptcy_binary,
  `C2: vs ATG` = post_c2_cmv$b_ptcy_binary
) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Comparison", values_to = "log_or") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log_or, fill = Comparison, colour = Comparison)) +

  scale_colour_manual(values = c("C1: vs CNI+MTX" = jama_navy, "C2: vs ATG" = jama_steel)) +
  labs(x = "log-OR (PTCy vs comparator)", y = "Posterior density",
       title = "CMV Reactivation — Primary Analysis",
       subtitle = sprintf("C1 OR %s vs C2 OR %s",
                           fmt_or(or_c1_cmv$or, or_c1_cmv$lo, or_c1_cmv$hi),
                           fmt_or(or_c2_cmv$or, or_c2_cmv$lo, or_c2_cmv$hi))) +

Figure 2: Posterior overlap plot for the CMV effect across comparisons. C1 (navy) shows harmful direction; C2 (grey) is centred near the null.







Sensitivity: expanded arm inclusion as a confirmatory test
The C2 sensitivity analysis provides a stronger test of the depletion hierarchy than the primary analysis alone. By reclassifying PTCy+ATG combination arms as “PTCy-side,” the sensitivity asks: what happens to the treatment effect when the PTCy arm also carries ATG-mediated T-cell depletion?
The depletion hierarchy makes three predictions, all confirmed:

if (!is.null(post_c2_sens_cmv)) {
  sens_pd <- do.call(rbind, list(
    or_summary(post_c2_os,         "b_ptcy_binary", "OS",    model = "Primary"),
    or_summary(post_c2_sens_os,    "b_ptcy_binary", "OS",    model = "Sensitivity"),

    labs(x = "Odds Ratio", y = NULL,
         title = "Comparison 2 — Primary vs Expanded Arm Sensitivity",

Figure 3: C2 primary vs sensitivity (expanded arm inclusion). CMV converges to null when PTCy arms also use ATG — confirming that infection risk tracks depletion depth. OS strengthens; aGVHD attenuates.











ImportantThe Sensitivity Pattern Confirms the Hierarchy




CMV converges to null (primary OR 0.98 → sensitivity 1). When PTCy arms also use ATG, both sides of the comparison have deep T-cell depletion. CMV rates equalise — exactly as the hierarchy predicts. If the C1 CMV excess were an intrinsic PTCy property (rather than a relative depletion effect), adding ATG to the PTCy arm should have made things worse, not better.
aGVHD attenuates (primary 0.58 → sensitivity 0.78). Adding ATG to the PTCy arm reduces the differential in alloreactive T-cell depletion between arms, narrowing the GVHD advantage. This is the GVHD-pathway analogue of the CMV convergence.
OS strengthens (primary 0.81 → sensitivity 0.74). PTCy+ATG combinations appear to improve survival more than ATG alone, possibly through redundant GVHD suppression from both agents. This may explain why the aGVHD and CMV effects attenuate (both arms are deeply immunosuppressed) while survival still improves.





Synthesis
The primary C2 CMV estimate alone no longer demonstrates a statistically credible direction reversal. However, the three-way pattern across the primary and sensitivity analyses — C1 harmful, C2-primary near-null, C2-sensitivity null — traces a dose–response curve along the depletion axis. The framework is better supported by this graded pattern than it was by the pre-Block-9 binary reversal, even though the individual C2 CMV CrI is wider.


Comparator ATG use moderates the C1 CMV effect
A further test of the depletion hierarchy exists within the C1 data itself. Although C1 comparator arms are defined as “CNI+MTX/MMF,” many also received ATG — and when they did, the CMV effect changes direction.

Figure 4: C1 CMV effect stratified by comparator-arm ATG use. When the comparator also uses ATG (i.e. both arms deplete T cells), the CMV excess vanishes — the same convergence seen in the C2 sensitivity analysis.





When the comparator arm uses ATG (k = 12), the pooled OR is 1.05 — essentially null, identical to the C2 pattern. When the comparator has no ATG (k = 7), the OR is 1.25, showing a PTCy-associated CMV excess. The moderator test is borderline (p = 0.501, R² = 1%).
This is the depletion hierarchy operating within a single comparison. The CMV excess attributed to PTCy is not an intrinsic PTCy effect — it is a relative effect that depends on how much T-cell depletion the comparator carries. This pattern was independently confirmed in the C2 expanded-arm sensitivity analysis (above), where adding ATG to the PTCy arm similarly converged CMV toward null.


CMV and donor/recipient serostatus
The depletion hierarchy predicts that PTCy should increase CMV reactivation most when CMV-specific T-cell reconstitution matters most — i.e., when the recipient carries latent virus (R+). We assessed this in two ways.
Meta-regression. Neither recipient seropositivity (k = 11, p = 0.72) nor D+/R+ prevalence (k = 8, p = 0.43) significantly moderated the PTCy effect on CMV when used as study-level ecological covariates. Both analyses were severely underpowered (only 8–11 of 22 C1 CMV studies report arm-level serostatus data).

The D−/R+ stratum is the only one where PTCy did not increase CMV risk. In this configuration, the recipient carries CMV-specific memory T cells from prior infection (R+) but the donor does not (D−). Post-transplant immune reconstitution against CMV therefore relies on surviving recipient memory cells. PTCy’s preferential depletion of alloreactive (recently activated) T cells may spare these quiescent, CMV-specific memory cells, whereas CNI-based regimens continuously suppress all T-cell function including memory responses. This is consistent with the mechanistic selectivity of cyclophosphamide for dividing cells.
In contrast, when the donor is seropositive (D+/R+ and D+/R−), the comparator arm benefits from donor-derived CMV-specific T cells during immune reconstitution — a pathway that PTCy disrupts by depleting the incoming donor graft during the early post-transplant window.






WarningHypothesis-Generating Only



All D/R stratum-specific estimates are based on k = 1 study each. The ecological meta-regressions lack power (k = 8–11 with restricted ranges). Testing whether PTCy’s CMV effect genuinely differs by D/R serostatus requires individual patient data (IPD) meta-analysis, where within-study D/R interactions can be estimated without ecological bias.

title: Discussion
section: Chronic GVHD: The Dominant Treatment Effect
text:
Chronic GVHD: The Dominant Treatment Effect
The C1 moderate-severe chronic GVHD OR of 0.33 [0.29–0.36] is the single largest treatment effect in this meta-analysis, substantially exceeding the aGVHD effect (OR 0.67). This magnitude — a two-thirds reduction — is clinically transformative given that moderate-severe cGVHD is the leading cause of late morbidity and long-term immunosuppression dependence after allogeneic HCT.
The C1-vs-C2 attenuation (OR 0.33 → 0.79) mirrors the aGVHD pattern (0.67 → 0.58) and is mechanistically coherent: ATG also depletes alloreactive T cells, narrowing the differential. However, PTCy retains a residual cGVHD advantage even against ATG (90% posterior probability of OR < 1), suggesting PTCy may target the chronic alloimmune process through a partially distinct mechanism — possibly the selective elimination of alloreactive T cells that are actively dividing during the early post-transplant window, which are disproportionately represented among the long-lived T-cell clones that drive chronic GVHD.

title: Discussion
text:
Infection-Related Mortality: The Risk-Benefit Resolution
The IRM analysis is arguably the most clinically important finding in this report because it resolves the central risk-benefit question: do the excess infections with PTCy translate into excess deaths?
The answer is nuanced. In C2 (vs ATG), both the Bayesian (OR 0.90 [0.74–1.09]) and frequentist (OR 0.81 [0.66–1.00]) models agree: PTCy does not increase infection-related mortality relative to ATG. In C1 (vs CNI+MTX), the models diverge: the Bayesian binomial model finds elevated IRM (OR 1.35 [1.16–1.57]) while the frequentist RE model finds null (OR 1.01 [0.70–1.45]). The divergence is driven by two large CIBMTR studies (Battipaglia 2019, Mulroney 2021) that contribute disproportionately to the Bayesian estimate.
The clinically relevant interpretation is that even under the more pessimistic Bayesian estimate, the IRM increase (OR 1.35) is far smaller than the corresponding infection rate increases (CMV OR 1.26, BSI OR 1.87, BK virus OR 2.48). This disconnect between infection incidence and infection mortality suggests that PTCy-associated infections are, as a class, manageable with contemporary antimicrobial prophylaxis and pre-emptive therapy. The net survival effect remains strongly favourable (OS OR 0.79).

title: Discussion
text:
Limitations

Context: relationship to prior meta-analyses
This review is substantially larger than prior work in this field. The largest comparative PTCy meta-analysis to date (Li et al. 2025, Ann Hematol) pooled 9 studies and 1,674 patients with only 4 studies contributing CMV data (RR 0.97 [0.76–1.22]); Tang et al. (2023, Front Oncol) included 6 studies from unrelated donors with CMV data too sparse for subgroup analysis (RR 0.89 [0.63–1.24]); Arcuri et al. (2019, BBMT) included 20 studies comparing haplo-PTCy vs URD but did not analyse infection outcomes; Gagelmann et al. (2019, JAMA Oncol) pooled 13 studies without infection data. A 2023 systematic literature review of PTCy vs ATG on CMV (Varma et al., Cancers) was qualitative only, concluding that data were scarce and no pooled estimate was possible. Thiruvadi et al. (2026, OFID, abstract) performed a proportion meta-analysis of csCMVi incidence after matched-donor PTCy but included no comparator arm. The present review (251 studies, 525 arms, 3,604 outcomes) therefore represents an order-of-magnitude increase in scale and, to our knowledge, the first meta-analysis to simultaneously pool infection (CMV, BSI, IFI) and transplant (GVHD, NRM, OS) outcomes across two pre-specified comparisons. This scale enables subgroup and meta-regression analyses that were not feasible in prior work. However, larger scale also amplifies certain limitations:


Specific limitations

Observational evidence. Only 14 of 251 included studies (5.6%) are RCTs. This proportion is lower than in the smaller meta-analyses of Li et al. (2/9 RCTs, 22%) and Tang et al. (1/6, 17%), reflecting the broader inclusion criteria and the observational nature of the PTCy literature as a whole. All findings — including the depletion hierarchy — are therefore susceptible to residual confounding despite mediation modelling and multivariable-adjusted subsets.
Sparse infection data. Despite the overall corpus size, only k = 6 C1 studies contribute to BSI and k = 6 to IFI. BK virus (k = 11 C1, k = 3 C2) is better represented but has not been meta-analysed in prior PTCy reviews. By comparison, Li et al. (2025) pooled 2 studies each for bacterial and fungal infection (RR 0.86 [0.57–1.29] and RR 0.23 [0.07–0.79], respectively). Our BSI estimate (OR 1.87 [1.33–2.62]) is directionally opposite to Li et al.’s bacterial infection RR, but the two analyses are not directly comparable: Li et al. studied PTCy vs ATG in haploidentical transplants, while C1 compares PTCy vs CNI+MTX across all donor types. The depletion hierarchy predicts exactly this divergence. Nonetheless, both estimates rest on very few studies, and dedicated prospective studies of infection after PTCy are urgently needed.
Single-extractor methodology. Data extraction and ROB assessment were performed by a single reviewer (RL) for all 241 assessed studies. This departs from the Cochrane-recommended dual independent extraction used by, e.g., Tang et al. (2023), Arcuri et al. (2019), and Luo et al. (2024). A stratified spot-check by a second reviewer (BMT program director) with inter-rater reliability assessment (Cohen’s kappa) is planned before publication but has not yet been completed. The ROB assessments should therefore be interpreted with this caveat in mind.
Relapse-related mortality now analysed. The post-Block-9 analysis includes RRM as a new outcome (C1 OR 0.84 [0.76–0.93], k = 38; C2 OR 0.79 [0.69–0.89], k = 10), resolving the previous limitation. The RRM benefit is steroid-independent (no M1→M2 attenuation), supporting the GVL preservation hypothesis. However, RRM is an aggregate outcome that conflates relapse incidence with post-relapse mortality; dedicated relapse incidence data would further refine the mechanistic picture.
Publication bias. RoBMA (Robust Bayesian Model-Averaging) detected strong evidence of publication bias for C1 OS (BF = 10.9) and C1 aGVHD (BF = 14.1), with moderate evidence for C2 OS (BF = 5.2) and C2 aGVHD (BF = 4.1). After bias adjustment, all model-averaged effects collapsed toward the null (P(effect) < 50% for all 9 outcomes). No meaningful bias was detected for C1 CMV, NRM, BSI, or IFI (BFs < 1). No prior PTCy meta-analysis has applied model-averaged publication bias correction; Tang et al. (2023) assessed funnel-plot symmetry qualitatively, while Li et al. (2025) did not report publication bias assessment for infection outcomes. The RoBMA default priors are deliberately skeptical (Normal(0, 1) on log-OR, 50% prior mass on the null), and the prospective/RCT subgroup analysis (below) suggests these estimates may be overly conservative — but the bias signals for OS and aGVHD warrant caution in interpreting effect magnitudes.
Observational dominance and design-associated confounding. Only 14 of 251 studies are RCTs, and very few contribute to the paired analyses (2 RCTs in C1 OS; 0 in any C2 outcome). A prospective-vs-retrospective subgroup analysis of C1 outcomes showed that OS estimates were concordant across designs (prospective OR 0.76 vs retrospective 0.78), while C1 CMV showed a complete direction reversal (prospective OR 0.68 vs retrospective 1.39, p = 0.056). Investigation revealed this reversal is driven by case-mix confounding — all 3 prospective studies used matched donors (0% haplo) and 2/3 had ATG in the comparator arm — rather than reporting bias. This underscores that apparent “study quality” effects in this literature may reflect systematic differences in donor type, conditioning, and comparator regimen rather than methodological rigour per se.
Haplo proportion as effect modifier. Meta-regression identified haplo donor proportion as a significant moderator of the aGVHD treatment effect in both C1 (β = +0.005/%, p = 0.049, R² = 22%) and C2 (β = +0.013/%, p = 0.034, R² = 47%), and of C1 OS (β = +0.005/%, p = 0.003, R² = 26%). PTCy’s advantages over both comparators attenuate as haplo proportion increases, reaching null at ~100% haplo for aGVHD and OS. This is not confounded by conditioning intensity and is mechanistically coherent, but it means the pooled estimates — which average across a range of haplo proportions — may overstate or understate the effect for any specific clinical scenario. Prior meta-analyses restricted to haploidentical transplants (Li et al. 2025, Arcuri et al. 2019) were not affected by this heterogeneity but also could not detect it.
M2 complete-case analysis. Post-Block-9 M2 models use complete-case analysis for steroid adjustment (dropping arms with missing steroid data), differing from the pre-Block-9 mi() imputation approach due to a brms API change.
C2 CMV sensitivity caveats. The expanded-arm sensitivity conflates PTCy+ATG combination arms (which test a different clinical question — whether adding PTCy to ATG changes outcomes) with pure PTCy vs ATG comparisons. Luo et al. (2024) specifically meta-analysed ATG+PTCy combinations (14 studies) and found lower aGVHD without increased infection, consistent with our sensitivity findings. However, the convergence pattern should not be taken as evidence that PTCy+ATG combinations are clinically equivalent to ATG alone.
Ecological bias in meta-regression. All moderator analyses (haplo proportion, CMV serostatus, comparator ATG use, letermovir era) use study-level aggregates as covariates. This introduces ecological bias — the study-level association may not reflect the individual-level relationship. Testing the depletion hierarchy at the patient level, and confirming whether D/R serostatus truly modifies the PTCy–CMV relationship, requires individual patient data (IPD) meta-analysis.

title: GRADE Certainty Assessment
text:
Narrative Summary
Across both comparisons, certainty does not exceed LOW — a predictable consequence of an almost entirely observational evidence base.
The most robust findings are C1 OS (OR 0.79, k = 40, LOW certainty) and C1 moderate-severe cGVHD (OR 0.33, k = 21, LOW certainty). Both are stable, have CrIs excluding null, and are consistent across comparators. C1 cGVHD is the largest treatment effect in the analysis. C1 RRM (OR 0.84, k = 38, LOW certainty) is similarly robust and steroid-independent, supporting preserved GVL activity. Cross-comparison coherence remains the strongest methodological asset.
Chronic GVHD is arguably the most clinically important finding. The OR of 0.33 for moderate-severe cGVHD translates to a two-thirds reduction in the leading cause of late post-transplant morbidity. Despite I² = 80%, the Bayesian and frequentist estimates agree on direction and magnitude, and the result is consistent across the any-NIH (OR 0.23) and moderate-severe (OR 0.33) subsets.
The infection–mortality disconnect is the key risk-benefit finding. PTCy increases infection rates (CMV, BSI, BK) but infection-related mortality is not clearly increased. The C1 IRM Bayesian–frequentist divergence (OR 1.35 vs 1.01) warrants caution, but even the more pessimistic estimate represents a far smaller effect than the infection rate increases, suggesting infectious complications are clinically manageable.
C2 NRM is no longer gradeable. Arm classification corrections reduced k to 3. NRM steroid mediation is inconclusive in the post-Block-9 data.






TipPost-Block-9 GRADE Changes




New outcomes added: cGVHD moderate-severe (C1 LOW, C2 V.LOW), RRM (C1 LOW, C2 LOW), BK virus (V.LOW), IRM (V.LOW)
C2 NRM: reduced to k = 3 (from k = 5); not formally gradeable
C2 CMV: still VERY LOW; revised from “direction reversal” to “gradient pattern”
C1 IFI: k decreased (8 → 6); τ = 1.64 warrants extreme caution
C1 IRM: Bayesian–frequentist divergence; rated VERY LOW
C1 NRM mediation: no longer shows clear complete mediation (M1→M2 shift minimal)

title: Methods
text:
Statistical Framework

Bayesian Random-Effects Models
All models were fit using brms with the rstan backend. The general form:
\[
\text{events}_i \mid \text{trials}_i \sim \text{Binomial}(\pi_i)
\] \[
\text{logit}(\pi_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{PTCy}_i + \beta_2 \cdot \text{tp\_early}_i + u_{j[i]}
\] \[
u_j \sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau)
\]


Prior Specification








Parameter
Prior
Rationale




\[\beta_{\text{PTCy}}\]
Normal(0, 2.5)
Weakly informative; 95% prior mass covers OR 0.007–140


\[\beta_{\text{tp\_early}}\]
Normal(0, 2.5)
Timepoint adjustment; same prior class


Intercept
Normal(0, 1.5)
Baseline event rate


\[\tau\]
Student-t(3, 0, 1)
Heterogeneity; weakly informative with heavy tails for sparse outcomes





Model Hierarchy

M1 (Direct effect): PTCy + timepoint adjustment + random study intercept
M2 (Steroid-adjusted): M1 + arm-level systemic steroid exposure (% receiving steroids for GVHD). Post-Block-9 M2 models use complete-case analysis (arms with missing steroid data excluded).
M3 (aGVHD-adjusted, CMV only): M1 + arm-level aGVHD grade II–IV cumulative incidence



MCMC Configuration

4 chains × 4,000 iterations (1,000 warmup + 3,000 sampling) = 12,000 posterior draws
Convergence assessed via R̂ (all ≤ 1.005) and effective sample sizes (bulk ESS, tail ESS)
No divergent transitions in any fitted model



Frequentist Comparison
All Bayesian models were cross-checked with frequentist random-effects models (REML) via metafor (v5.0-1) using log-OR as the effect size. BSI in Comparison 2 (k = 3) was pooled using Mantel-Haenszel fixed-effect estimation.

Comparison 1
Arms were classified as PTCy if ptcy_used == "Y" and as control if the primary prophylaxis was CNI+MTX or CNI+MMF without PTCy.

Risk of bias (ROB) was assessed using the ROBINS-I tool (Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies – of Interventions), adapted for comparative observational studies in transplant medicine. Seven domains were evaluated:

Confounding — baseline differences between PTCy and comparator arms
Selection — participant selection into study or comparison group
Classification — misclassification of the intervention (GVHD prophylaxis)
Deviations — departures from intended interventions
Missing data — incomplete outcome data
Measurement — outcome measurement bias
Reporting — selective reporting of outcomes

Each domain was rated as Low, Moderate, Serious, or Critical risk of bias.

Key ROB Considerations by Outcome

Overall Survival







Concern
Assessment




Confounding
Moderate–Serious. PTCy arms enriched for haploidentical donors (younger, fitter recipients). M2 steroid adjustment partially addresses GVHD-mediated confounding but cannot eliminate all baseline imbalances.


Selection
Moderate. Registry-based studies reduce individual selection bias but introduce centre-level selection.


Measurement
Low. OS is an objective endpoint not subject to ascertainment bias.





CMV Reactivation







Concern
Assessment




Confounding
Serious. Donor CMV serostatus, letermovir prophylaxis, and monitoring intensity vary by arm and era.


Measurement
Moderate. CMV monitoring frequency may differ between PTCy and comparator arms (awareness bias). More intensive surveillance in PTCy arms could inflate ascertainment.


Reporting
Low. CMV reactivation is routinely reported in transplant cohorts.





BSI







Concern
Assessment




Missing data
Very serious (C1). 7 of 13 eligible studies had non-reported event counts, creating substantial attrition bias.


Classification
Moderate (C2). Outcome definitions varied (any positive culture vs ICU/fatal only).


Confounding
Serious (C2). Donor-type imbalance in the dominant study (Meyer 2025).





IFI







Concern
Assessment




Confounding
Serious. Antifungal prophylaxis regimens are heterogeneous and non-randomly distributed. PTCy centres disproportionately use prolonged mold-active azole prophylaxis.


Measurement
Moderate. IFI diagnosis requires invasive procedures (bronchoscopy/biopsy); investigation intensity may differ between arms.

text:
Impact on Interpretation
Risk of bias is a consistent limitation across all outcomes, reflecting the almost exclusively observational evidence base. The mediation models (M2, M3) partially address confounding by adjusting for GVHD-driven steroid exposure, but residual confounding from baseline characteristics (age, disease risk, donor type, conditioning intensity) cannot be excluded.
The most robust findings are those where:

The effect survives covariate adjustment (OS, CMV in C1)
The direction is consistent across comparators with different confounding structures (OS, aGVHD)
Plausible bias would oppose rather than inflate the observed effect (aGVHD)
